definition:
The gifts of the Spirit are the abilities and ministries God gives to members of his people so that they can serve one another and build up the church. Paul's rule for all of them is short: “to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:7). Some gifts look ordinary, such as teaching, serving, giving, leading, helping, and showing mercy. Others are plainly extraordinary, such as healing, miracles, prophecy, and speaking in tongues. Scripture never ranks the first kind as less spiritual than the second. The gifts are distinct from the gift of the Spirit himself, whom every believer receives (Acts 2:38), and distinct from the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23), the character he grows in every believer. Christians agree on all of this. They differ on whether some gifts, especially prophecy, tongues, and gifts of healing, continue in the church today, and that is a second-order question on which faithful believers who share the same gospel have landed in different places.

The main Greek word is charisma, a gift freely given. It is formed from the verb charizomai, ‘to give freely’, and is related to charis, ‘grace’, and Paul draws on that connection when he says “We have different gifts according to the grace given us” (Romans 12:6). The word occurs seventeen times in the New Testament, sixteen of them in Paul's letters and once in 1 Peter 4:10, and its range is wider than the modern phrase ‘spiritual gifts’: Paul uses it of eternal life (Romans 6:23), of the ability to live unmarried (1 Corinthians 7:7), and of God's gifts to Israel (Romans 11:29). Paul also speaks of pneumatika, ‘spiritual things’ or ‘spiritual gifts’ (1 Corinthians 12:1; 14:1), probably the Corinthians' own favored word; of diakoniai, ‘ministries’ or ‘services’, and energēmata, ‘workings’ (1 Corinthians 12:5-6); and of phanerōsis, the ‘manifestation’ of the Spirit (12:7). In Ephesians 4:8 the word is domata, ‘gifts’, and the gifts are people: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers given by the ascended Christ to his church.
ot:
The Old Testament does not use a technical word for spiritual gifts, but it lays the foundation by showing God's Spirit equipping people for service. The first person said to be filled with the Spirit of God is Bezalel, and the gift is “skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3). God also gives him and Oholiab “the ability to teach others” (Exodus 35:34), so from the start a gift is meant to spread to others and to serve the worship of God's people. When Moses cannot carry the people alone, God places some of the Spirit that is on him on seventy elders, with the promise to Moses that “They will help you bear the burden of the people” (Numbers 11:17). The judges receive the Spirit to lead and deliver (Judges 3:10; 6:34), Saul and David to rule (1 Samuel 10:6; 16:13), and the prophets to speak God's word (2 Samuel 23:2; Micah 3:8). Each of these gifts is for others: for the tabernacle, the burdened people, the oppressed tribes, the kingdom, the covenant community that needed to hear.

The Old Testament also shows that such gifts are not guarantees of character. Samson's strength coexisted with recklessness, and the Spirit's departure from him was a loss he did not notice (Judges 16:20). Saul prophesied and still lost his kingdom. Balaam, a hired seer, spoke true oracles while serving his own interest (Numbers 22 to 24). The law provided tests for prophets, whose words had to come true and had to keep Israel loyal to the LORD (Deuteronomy 13:1-5; 18:21-22). These patterns stand behind the New Testament's insistence that gifts be tested and exercised in love.

The prophets promised a wider distribution. Moses had wished “that all the LORD's people were prophets” (Numbers 11:29), and Joel announced that God would pour out his Spirit on sons and daughters, old and young, and servants, so that they would prophesy, dream dreams, and see visions (Joel 2:28-29). Isaiah foretold a king on whom the Spirit would rest as “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:2). The Greek and Latin translations of Isaiah 11:2-3 render the fear of the LORD in two ways, one of them as ‘piety’, and so give seven names, which later Christian tradition called the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Psalm 68:18 pictures God ascending in triumph and receiving gifts; Paul quotes it with the verb changed to give, “He led captives away, and gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8), a reading also found in the Aramaic Targum of the Psalms, which in its surviving form is later than Paul and applies the verse to Moses giving the law. Paul reads the psalm as fulfilled in the ascended Christ, who now distributes gifts to his people.
nt:
In the Gospels, Jesus gives the Twelve “power and authority over all demons, and power to cure diseases” (Luke 9:1) and sends seventy-two others to heal the sick and announce the kingdom (Luke 10:9). He also warns that gifts are not proof of belonging to him: some will say they prophesied and did miracles in his name, and he will answer, “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:22-23). At Pentecost the Spirit gives the disciples power to speak in other languages that pilgrims from many lands understand (Acts 2:4-11). Acts goes on to show the gifts spreading beyond the apostles. Stephen, one of seven chosen because they were “full of the Spirit and wisdom” (Acts 6:3) to oversee the daily distribution to widows, also performs “great wonders and signs” (Acts 6:8), and Philip heals in Samaria (Acts 8:6-7). The church at Antioch has “prophets and teachers” (Acts 13:1); Agabus predicts a famine and later Paul's arrest (Acts 11:28; 21:10-11); Philip has “four unmarried daughters who prophesied” (Acts 21:9). The Holy Spirit falls on the household of Cornelius and they speak in tongues (Acts 10:46), a sign to Peter's companions that Gentiles had received the same gift.

Paul gives the church its fullest teaching, and he gives it in lists that differ from one another. Romans 12:6-8 names prophecy, serving, teaching, encouraging, giving, leading, and showing mercy. First Corinthians 12:8-10 names the message of wisdom, the message of knowledge, faith, gifts of healing, miracles, prophecy, distinguishing between spirits, tongues, and the interpretation of tongues. First Corinthians 12:28 names apostles, prophets, teachers, miracles, healing, helping, administration, and tongues. Ephesians 4:11 names apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers (the Greek grammar allows ‘pastors and teachers’ to be one role or two closely joined). Peter reduces the whole to two kinds, speaking and serving (1 Peter 4:10-11). No list repeats another, none claims to be complete, and they mix what modern readers would call natural abilities with the plainly miraculous. The lists illustrate; they do not catalogue. Paul also speaks of gifts given through prophecy and the laying on of hands, which Timothy is to use and “fan into flame” (1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6).

The longest discussion, 1 Corinthians 12 to 14, was written to a church that prized speaking in tongues as a mark of spiritual status. Paul answers in three movements. First, the gifts come from one Spirit, one Lord, and one God (12:4-6), and the Spirit “apportions them to each one as He determines” (12:11), so no one chooses a gift or boasts in it. The church is a body, and “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I do not need you’” (12:21); the weaker-seeming members are “indispensable” (12:22), and the string of questions that begins “Are all apostles?” and includes “Do all speak in tongues?” (12:29-30) expects the answer no. Second, without love every gift is worthless: tongues become “a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal” (13:1). Love outlasts the gifts, because “we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away” (13:9-10). Third, gifts in the gathering must build up the church, the Greek word being oikodomē, ‘building’ or ‘edification’. Prophecy speaks to people “for their edification, encouragement, and comfort” (14:3), while an uninterpreted tongue builds up only the speaker (14:4). Paul thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than all of them, but in church he would rather speak “five coherent words” than ten thousand in a tongue (14:18-19). Tongues must be interpreted, prophets must speak in turn and “the others should weigh carefully what is said” (14:29), and “everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner” (14:40). He concludes, “be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues” (14:39). In 1 Thessalonians the same balance appears: “Do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things. Hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:20-21).

Several questions in these chapters remain open among careful readers. Tongues at Pentecost were human languages the hearers recognized; in Corinth they need interpretation, and the one who speaks in a tongue “does not speak to men, but to God” (14:2); Paul also mentions “the tongues of men and of angels” (13:1), so some hold that tongues are always human languages and others that they may also be a Spirit-given language of prayer. Prophecy in the New Testament may be the same kind of speech as Old Testament prophecy, carrying God's full authority, or a lesser kind that reports what the Spirit brings to mind and must be weighed; Wayne Grudem's The Gift of Prophecy in the New Testament and Today (1988) argued for the second view and many cessationists answer with the first. And the phrase “when the perfect comes” (13:10) has been read as the return of Christ, which most commentators on all sides now accept, as the completion of the New Testament, which some cessationists hold, or as the church's maturity. Hebrews 2:3-4 adds that God confirmed the gospel through the first hearers “through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His will”, a text cessationists stress. Whatever the answers, the New Testament's governing concerns are clear: every believer has some gift, gifts are for others, love is the more excellent way, and the Spirit, not the gifted person, receives the glory.

keyTexts.why: Bezalel is filled with the Spirit of God for craftsmanship in building the tabernacle. The Spirit's gifts include skills of the hand, given to serve the worship of God's people.
God shares the Spirit on Moses with seventy elders so that they can bear the people's burden with him, and Moses wishes that all God's people were prophets.
The promise that God will pour out his Spirit on all his people, so that sons and daughters prophesy. Peter quotes it at Pentecost.
The Spirit is poured out and the disciples speak in languages that hearers from many nations understand. Peter explains the event as the fulfillment of Joel.
Gifts differ according to grace and belong to one body. Paul's list includes serving, teaching, encouraging, giving, leading, and mercy alongside prophecy.
One Spirit, one Lord, and one God give varied gifts, each for the common good, apportioned as the Spirit determines. The fullest single list of gifts.
The church as a body in which every member is needed and the weaker parts are indispensable. Not all have the same gift.
Without love every gift is empty, and love outlasts the gifts that belong to this partial age. The central text in the debate over whether some gifts cease.
Gifts in the gathering must build up the church. Paul orders tongues and prophecy, requires interpretation and weighing, and forbids neither.
The ascended Christ gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers to equip the saints for ministry, so the whole body grows up in love.
Do not extinguish the Spirit or despise prophecies, but test everything and hold fast to what is good. Openness and discernment are commanded together.
God confirmed the gospel spoken by the first hearers with signs, wonders, miracles, and gifts of the Spirit. Cessationists read it as tying the sign gifts to the founding generation.
Each believer is a steward of God's varied grace, using whatever gift he has received to serve others in speech or service, so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ.

history:
The early church expected the Spirit's gifts and learned to test them. The Didache, a church manual usually dated between about AD 50 and 120, tells congregations how to receive traveling apostles and prophets and how to recognize false ones by their conduct, such as asking for money (chapters 11 to 13). Justin Martyr told the Jewish teacher Trypho, in the middle of the second century, that prophetic gifts remained among Christians (Dialogue with Trypho 82), and Irenaeus of Lyons, about 180, wrote that he had heard many in the church who had prophetic gifts and spoke in all kinds of languages through the Spirit (Against Heresies 5.6.1). In the later second century the Montanist movement in Phrygia, led by Montanus and the prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla, claimed a new outpouring of prophecy that went beyond the apostles, and the church's rejection of it made later leaders wary of claims to new revelation. By the late fourth century John Chrysostom, preaching on 1 Corinthians 12 (Homily 29), said the passage was obscure because the gifts it described no longer occurred. Augustine early in his career wrote that the miraculous signs of the apostolic age had not continued, but in The City of God (22.8) he recorded healings in his own North African church, and in his Retractations he qualified his earlier statement.

Medieval theology distinguished the grace that makes a person pleasing to God from graces freely given for the benefit of others, and Thomas Aquinas in the Summa Theologiae (I-II, question 111) placed Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 12 among the second, gifts that serve others and do not in themselves make the gifted person holy. He also treated the seven gifts drawn from Isaiah 11 as dispositions given to every person in grace. The Reformers recovered the conviction that every believer has a calling; Martin Luther's To the Christian Nobility (1520) argued that all baptized Christians share in the priesthood. John Calvin taught that apostles, prophets, and evangelists were offices God raised up at the beginning of his kingdom and could raise up again in times of necessity, while pastors and teachers are the ordinary and permanent offices (Institutes 4.3.4). The Westminster Confession (1646) teaches that the former ways by which God revealed his will to his people have now ceased, now that Scripture is complete (1.1). John Owen's posthumous discourse on spiritual gifts (1693) distinguished extraordinary gifts belonging to the church's founding from ordinary gifts that continue for its ministry.

In modern times the question became sharp. B. B. Warfield's Counterfeit Miracles (1918) argued that the miraculous gifts were the credentials of the apostles and passed away with them. At almost the same time the Pentecostal movement, beginning with Charles Parham's school in Topeka (1901) and the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles (1906) under William J. Seymour, taught that tongues, prophecy, and healing belonged to the church of every age. The charismatic renewal brought these experiences into historic Protestant churches from about 1960 and into the Roman Catholic Church from 1967. The Second Vatican Council's Lumen Gentium (1964, section 12) taught that the Spirit distributes special graces among the faithful of every rank, that ordinary charisms are to be received with thanksgiving, that extraordinary gifts are not to be rashly sought, and that judging their genuineness belongs to those who lead the church. In the 1980s John Wimber and C. Peter Wagner spoke of a Third Wave of the Spirit among evangelicals who did not identify as Pentecostal or charismatic. Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views (1996), edited by Wayne Grudem, set four positions side by side: cessationist (Richard Gaffin), open but cautious (Robert Saucy), Third Wave (Sam Storms), and Pentecostal and charismatic (Douglas Oss). Meanwhile churches of every tradition have taught that each member has gifts for ministry. The site's page on the Holy Spirit and his gifts sets out the positions at greater length.

differ.body: Cessationists hold that the Spirit still gives every gift needed for the church's life, such as teaching, leading, serving, and mercy, and that God still answers prayer for healing, but that the revelatory and sign gifts (apostleship, prophecy, tongues, and gifts of healing and miracles as gifts residing in individuals) belonged to the church's founding. The church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. Signs marked the apostles (2 Corinthians 12:12) and confirmed the message of the first hearers (Hebrews 2:3-4), and with the completion of the New Testament, Scripture is sufficient. They add that genuine prophecy in the Bible spoke with God's authority and so could not be fallible, and that what goes by the name today does not meet that standard. Richard Gaffin, John MacArthur, and the Warfield tradition hold versions of this view, and many cessationists accept that the “perfect” of 1 Corinthians 13:10 is the return of Christ, resting their case on other texts.

Many evangelicals find the arguments for cessation not strong enough to rule the gifts out and the practice of many churches not careful enough to embrace them unreservedly. Nothing in the New Testament says in so many words that particular gifts would end before Christ's return, so they will not tell God what he may not give. Yet the extraordinary gifts seem to cluster at great moments of revelation, and much that is claimed as prophecy or healing today is doubtful, so they do not seek such gifts as normal and they test everything (1 Thessalonians 5:21). The emphasis falls on the ordinary gifts, on Scripture's sufficiency, and on love. Robert Saucy represented this view in the 1996 four-views volume.

Evangelicals in this stream, associated with John Wimber, the Vineyard movement, and writers such as Sam Storms, hold that all the gifts described in the New Testament continue and should be sought, because Paul commands the church to “eagerly desire spiritual gifts, especially the gift of prophecy” (1 Corinthians 14:1) and not to forbid tongues (14:39), and because the “perfect” that ends partial knowledge is the face-to-face sight of the last day (13:10-12). They understand congregational prophecy as a real prompting of the Spirit that is spoken humbly and weighed by the church (14:29), never equal to Scripture. Unlike classical Pentecostals, they hold that every believer receives the Spirit at conversion and that tongues are one gift among many, not the required sign of a second experience.

Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, now a large share of the world's believers, hold that the church lives in the “last days” in which God pours out his Spirit on all people (Acts 2:17), that the promise is “to all who are far off” (Acts 2:39), and that the Book of Acts shows what the Spirit-filled church is meant to be. Tongues, prophecy, healing, and miracles belong to the normal equipment of the church for worship and mission until Christ returns. Classical Pentecostals add that believers should seek a baptism in the Spirit, evidenced by tongues, which empowers them for witness; many charismatics in historic churches share the expectation of the gifts without that teaching. They answer the objection of abuse as Paul did in Corinth: by ordering the gifts, not forbidding them. Douglas Oss represented this view in the 1996 volume.

errors:
Scripture itself names several distortions of the gifts. Simon in Samaria tried to buy the power to give the Spirit, and Peter answered, “you thought you could buy the gift of God with money” (Acts 8:20); the church named the buying and selling of spiritual things simony after him and has condemned it ever since. The Corinthians treated gifts as marks of rank, and Paul answered that every member is needed and that gifts without love are nothing (1 Corinthians 12 to 13). Jesus warned that prophecy and miracles done in his name do not prove that a person knows him (Matthew 7:22-23), so a gift must never be mistaken for godliness or used to shield a leader from accountability. The early church rejected Montanism's claim that new prophecy could go beyond the apostles, and every tradition holds that no claimed revelation may add to or contradict Scripture.

Other errors are pastoral. Teaching that promises healing to everyone with enough faith, or that ties gifts to money given, burdens the sick with guilt and turns grace into a transaction; Scripture shows Paul leaving Trophimus sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20), advising Timothy about his frequent ailments (1 Timothy 5:23), and hearing the Lord say “My grace is sufficient for you” when his own thorn was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:9). On the other side, a church can despise what it does not understand; Paul forbids treating prophecies with contempt and forbids quenching the Spirit (1 Thessalonians 5:19-20). Cessationists and continuationists both reject contempt for fellow believers across this line, since the question is second-order. A last error is quieter: treating ministry as the work of a gifted few while the rest watch, when Paul says the leaders are given “to equip the saints for works of ministry” (Ephesians 4:12).
life:
The doctrine of the gifts means that no believer is without a part to play. The Spirit gives “to each one” (1 Corinthians 12:7), and the gifts that seem weakest are indispensable. The person who prepares meals for a grieving family, keeps the books honestly, teaches children, visits prisoners, or prays faithfully in obscurity is exercising gifts the Spirit gave for the body's good. Most people learn their gifts not by filling out an inventory but by serving where there is need and listening to how the church is helped.

It also means that gifts are held with humility. They are given, not earned, and given for others, not for the person who has them. That frees believers from envy of someone else's gift and from pride in their own. Whatever a church believes about tongues and prophecy, the path Paul calls “the most excellent way” (1 Corinthians 12:31) is open to all of them: love that is patient and kind, that builds others up, and that will remain when every partial gift has passed away.
questions: Paul's lists of gifts in Romans 12, 1 Corinthians 12, Ephesians 4, and 1 Peter 4 differ from one another. What does that suggest about how to think of gifts, and about gifts not named in any list?
Why does Paul place the chapter on love (1 Corinthians 13) in the middle of his teaching on gifts? What would change in a church that took that placement seriously?
Christians differ on whether prophecy and tongues continue today. What do all sides agree about, and how can believers who disagree serve together with respect?
